items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The amount of a renewable resource, such as fish or timber, that can be taken without reducing future supply"?
items.answer: sustainable yield
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of sustainable yield.

items.stem: Explain the difference between reserves and resources.
items.answer: Resources are the total amount that exists; reserves are the part that is known and economically extractable with current technology.
items.markingKey: Resources are the total amount that exists; reserves are the part that is known and economically extractable with current technology. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Renewable resources can never run out." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Biological renewable resources such as fish and forests can be destroyed if used faster than they regrow; only flow resources like sunlight and wind are effectively unlimited.
items.markingKey: Biological renewable resources such as fish and forests can be destroyed if used faster than they regrow; only flow resources like sunlight and wind are effectively unlimited. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The Newfoundland northern cod spawning stock went from 1,600 thousand tonnes in 1962 to 22 thousand tonnes in 1992. Which is the percentage change?

A class brainstorm on renewable and non-renewable resources produced the question "Will resources run out?" Explain why it needs refining, then suggest an improved research question and justify your change.
items.answer: Weakness: it is vague (which resources, where, when?) and too broad Improved: "How sustainable is the use of groundwater for irrigation in the Punjab region of India?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is vague (which resources, where, when?) and too broad); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How sustainable is the use of groundwater for irrigation in the Punjab region of India?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem:
Source A – Government report (paraphrased): Paraphrase of the announcement by the Canadian Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, 2 July 1992

The minister announced a moratorium on the northern cod fishery. Scientists had found that the spawning stock had fallen to the lowest level ever measured. The closure would affect thousands of fishers and plant workers, and the government would provide income support.

"Renewable resources will solve the problem of resource scarcity." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: They can greatly reduce scarcity in energy, but only with sustainable management and reduced consumption, since they depend on finite minerals and fragile ecosystems.
items.markingKey: From the source: Cod stocks had collapsed, so the fishery was closed despite the economic cost. Own knowledge for: wind, solar and hydro can replace fossil fuels for energy; managed forests and fisheries can supply resources indefinitely. Own knowledge against: renewable technologies need non-renewable minerals such as lithium, cobalt and copper; renewable biological resources can be over-used. Judgement: They can greatly reduce scarcity in energy, but only with sustainable management and reduced consumption, since they depend on finite minerals and fragile ecosystems. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "resource depletion".
items.answer: The using up of a resource faster than it is replaced
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the using up of a resource faster than it is replaced. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why renewable resources can still be used unsustainably.
items.answer: If they are used faster than they regenerate – over-fishing, deforestation, over-pumping aquifers – stocks fall and may collapse, as with Newfoundland cod.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If they are used faster than they regenerate – over-fishing, deforestation, over-pumping aquifers – stocks fall and may collapse, as with Newfoundland cod. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Recycling makes non-renewable resources renewable." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Recycling metals extends supplies and reduces mining, but losses occur and the resource does not regenerate naturally.
items.markingKey: Recycling metals extends supplies and reduces mining, but losses occur and the resource does not regenerate naturally. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into renewable and non-renewable resources?

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How sustainable is the use of groundwater for irrigation in the Punjab region of India?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Collect Central Ground Water Board data on water-table depth; read two reports; map affected districts; calculate the rate of fall; compare with recharge; evaluate data sources; cite in APA.

items.stem: Which accident in 2011 led Germany to decide to close its nuclear power stations?
options: Three Mile Island in the USA
items.answer: Fukushima Daiichi in Japan
items.markingKey: B. Germany closed its last plants in April 2023.

items.stem: Briefly explain why some countries depend heavily on imported energy.
items.answer: They lack domestic reserves of fossil fuels or suitable renewable sites, so they must buy energy, which affects their energy security – as Europe found when gas prices rose in 2022.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They lack domestic reserves of fossil fuels or suitable renewable sites, so they must buy energy, which affects their energy security – as Europe found when gas prices rose in 2022. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between non-renewable energy and renewable energy.
items.answer: Renewable energy comes from sources that are replenished naturally (sun, wind, water, geothermal); non-renewable energy comes from finite stocks (coal, oil, gas, uranium).
items.markingKey: Renewable energy comes from sources that are replenished naturally (sun, wind, water, geothermal); non-renewable energy comes from finite stocks (coal, oil, gas, uranium). items.stem: The ecological footprint of a family in the United States is estimated at 8.0 global hectares (gha) per person, close to the national average. The Earth's biocapacity is about 1.6 gha per person. How many Earths would be needed if everyone lived this way? Comment on what this means for sustainability.
items.answer: 5.00 Earths
items.markingKey: 8.0 ÷ 1.6 = 5.00 Earths (M1 A1). Comment (R1): above 1 means consumption exceeds what the planet can regenerate (ecological overshoot); below 1 is within limits.

items.stem: Jonas argues that "Countries should stop using fossil fuels immediately." Elena disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: A rapid but managed transition is more realistic than an immediate stop, with richer countries moving fastest and supporting others.
items.markingKey: Jonas: burning fossil fuels is the main cause of climate change. Elena: an immediate stop would cause energy shortages and economic harm, especially in poorer countries. Judgement (1-2 marks): A rapid but managed transition is more realistic than an immediate stop, with richer countries moving fastest and supporting others.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Countries should stop using fossil fuels immediately."
items.answer: A rapid but managed transition is more realistic than an immediate stop, with richer countries moving fastest and supporting others.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: burning fossil fuels is the main cause of climate change; renewables are now the cheapest source of new electricity in most places. Arguments against: an immediate stop would cause energy shortages and economic harm, especially in poorer countries; grids, storage and industry need time to change. Supported judgement: A rapid but managed transition is more realistic than an immediate stop, with richer countries moving fastest and supporting others.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Countries should stop using fossil fuels immediately." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "energy security"?
options: A resource that is naturally replaced within a human lifetime, such as solar energy, wind or timber if managed
Having reliable, affordable access to enough energy
The order of preference for managing waste: reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, and finally dispose
A fuel formed over millions of years from the remains of plants and animals, such as coal, oil and natural gas
items.answer: Having reliable, affordable access to enough energy
items.markingKey: B. "energy security" is having reliable, affordable access to enough energy.

items.stem: Explain why the cost of solar power has fallen so much.
items.answer: Mass production (especially in China), technological improvements in panel efficiency and economies of scale cut the cost of solar electricity by around 90% between 2010 and 2020.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Mass production (especially in China), technological improvements in panel efficiency and economies of scale cut the cost of solar electricity by around 90% between 2010 and 2020. items.stem: "Renewables can only ever supply a small share of electricity." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Some countries already get most of their electricity from renewables – e.g. Norway (mostly hydro), Iceland, Costa Rica and Uruguay.
items.markingKey: Some countries already get most of their electricity from renewables – e.g. Norway (mostly hydro), Iceland, Costa Rica and Uruguay. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to Iceland's geothermal energy, explain how it illustrates physical geography shaping the energy mix.
items.answer: Iceland uses geothermal heat for about 90% of home heating and, with hydropower, for nearly all its electricity. Its position on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge gives abundant renewable heat.

items.stem: 2022 estimates: Nigeria – 130 Mt CO₂, 219 million people; Japan – 1,050 Mt CO₂, 125 million people. Calculate per-capita emissions for each and explain why total and per-capita figures can lead to different conclusions about responsibility for climate change.

items.stem:
Source A – Report extract (paraphrased): Paraphrase of the World Commission on Environment and Development, "Our Common Future" (the Brundtland Report), 1987

The commission defined sustainable development as development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It stressed that the needs of the world's poor should be given overriding priority.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching sustainable living: reduce, reuse, recycle and the ecological footprint? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of the World Commission on Environment and Development, "Our Common Future" (the Brundtland Report), 1987. Purpose: to set out a global vision linking environment and development for governments. Value: It is the source of the most widely used definition of sustainable development. Limitation: It is a statement of principles agreed by a commission and gives no measurable targets or ways to enforce them.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of the World Commission on Environment and Development, "Our Common Future" (the Brundtland Report), 1987. Purpose: to set out a global vision linking environment and development for governments. Value: It is the source of the most widely used definition of sustainable development. Limitation: It is a statement of principles agreed by a commission and gives no measurable targets or ways to enforce them. Award up to [3]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ecological footprint"?

The amount of a renewable resource, such as fish or timber, that can be taken without reducing future supply
The date each year when humanity's demand for resources exceeds what the Earth can regenerate in that year
The area of productive land and water needed to supply the resources a person or population uses and absorb its waste, measured in global hectares
items.answer: The area of productive land and water needed to supply the resources a person or population uses and absorb its waste, measured in global hectares
items.markingKey: D. "ecological footprint" is the area of productive land and water needed to supply the resources a person or population uses and absorb its waste, measured in global hectares.

items.stem:
Source A – Government report (paraphrased): Paraphrase of the announcement by the Canadian Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, 2 July 1992

The minister announced a moratorium on the northern cod fishery. Scientists had found that the spawning stock had fallen to the lowest level ever measured. The closure would affect thousands of fishers and plant workers, and the government would provide income support.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching renewable and non-renewable resources? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of the announcement by the Canadian Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, 2 July 1992. Purpose: to announce and justify the closure of the fishery to the public and to fishing communities. Value: It is the official announcement and shows the scientific evidence the government relied on. Limitation: As a government statement it does not discuss why earlier warnings and quotas failed.

items.stem:
Source A – Report extract (paraphrased): Paraphrase of the World Commission on Environment and Development, "Our Common Future" (the Brundtland Report), 1987

The commission defined sustainable development as development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It stressed that the needs of the world's poor should be given overriding priority.

"Individuals are mainly responsible for making lifestyles more sustainable." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Individuals have a role, but governments and businesses carry the greater responsibility because they shape the systems within which individuals choose.
items.markingKey: From the source: Development must meet present needs, especially of the poor, without harming future generations. Own knowledge for: consumer choices about food, travel and waste shape demand; collective individual action can change markets. Own knowledge against: about 70% of industrial emissions since 1988 have been linked to around 100 fossil-fuel producers (CDP 2017); governments set the rules and infrastructure that make sustainable choices possible. Judgement: Individuals have a role, but governments and businesses carry the greater responsibility because they shape the systems within which individuals choose. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem:
Source A – Energy agency report (paraphrased): Summary of International Energy Agency (IEA), "Renewables 2023" report, January 2024

The agency reported that the world added a record amount of renewable power capacity in 2023, about 50% more than in 2022, with solar accounting for about three-quarters of the additions. China alone commissioned as much solar capacity as the entire world did in 2022.

"Countries should stop using fossil fuels immediately." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: A rapid but managed transition is more realistic than an immediate stop, with richer countries moving fastest and supporting others.
items.markingKey: From the source: Renewable capacity grew at record speed in 2023, led by solar and by China. Own knowledge for: burning fossil fuels is the main cause of climate change; renewables are now the cheapest source of new electricity in most places. Own knowledge against: an immediate stop would cause energy shortages and economic harm, especially in poorer countries; grids, storage and industry need time to change. Judgement: A rapid but managed transition is more realistic than an immediate stop, with richer countries moving fastest and supporting others. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Renewable resources will solve the problem of resource scarcity."
items.answer: Thesis: They can greatly reduce scarcity in energy, but only with sustainable management and reduced consumption, since they depend on finite minerals and fragile ecosystems.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: wind, solar and hydro can replace fossil fuels for energy; managed forests and fisheries can supply resources indefinitely. Counter-arguments: renewable technologies need non-renewable minerals such as lithium, cobalt and copper; renewable biological resources can be over-used. Thesis/conclusion: They can greatly reduce scarcity in energy, but only with sustainable management and reduced consumption, since they depend on finite minerals and fragile ecosystems. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Define the term "fossil fuel".
items.answer: A fuel formed over millions of years from the remains of plants and animals, such as coal, oil and natural gas
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a fuel formed over millions of years from the remains of plants and animals, such as coal, oil and natural gas. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "renewable resource"?
options: Electricity generated from the heat released by splitting uranium atoms
A resource that is naturally replaced within a human lifetime, such as solar energy, wind or timber if managed
The amount of a renewable resource, such as fish or timber, that can be taken without reducing future supply
The total greenhouse gas emissions caused by a person, product or organisation
items.answer: A resource that is naturally replaced within a human lifetime, such as solar energy, wind or timber if managed
items.markingKey: B. "renewable resource" is a resource that is naturally replaced within a human lifetime, such as solar energy, wind or timber if managed.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs"?
items.answer: sustainability
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of sustainability.

items.stem: "Nuclear power is a fossil fuel." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Nuclear power uses uranium, a non-renewable mineral, but does not burn fuel and emits very little CO₂ during operation.
items.markingKey: Nuclear power uses uranium, a non-renewable mineral, but does not burn fuel and emits very little CO₂ during operation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why resource extraction can lead to conflict.
items.answer: Valuable resources can fund armed groups, cause disputes over who benefits, and damage land and water used by local communities.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Valuable resources can fund armed groups, cause disputes over who benefits, and damage land and water used by local communities. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between carbon footprint and ecological footprint.
items.answer: An ecological footprint measures all the land and sea area needed to support consumption; a carbon footprint measures only greenhouse gas emissions.
items.markingKey: An ecological footprint measures all the land and sea area needed to support consumption; a carbon footprint measures only greenhouse gas emissions. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why wind and solar power create challenges for electricity grids.
items.answer: Their output varies with the weather and time of day, so grids need storage (batteries, pumped hydro), backup power or wider connections to balance supply and demand.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Their output varies with the weather and time of day, so grids need storage (batteries, pumped hydro), backup power or wider connections to balance supply and demand. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why the size of reserves of a non-renewable resource can increase.
items.answer: New discoveries, better technology (e.g. fracking) and higher prices can make more deposits economic to extract, even though the total amount in the ground is fixed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: New discoveries, better technology (e.g. fracking) and higher prices can make more deposits economic to extract, even though the total amount in the ground is fixed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Individual choices make no difference to sustainability." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Individual choices add up and influence markets, though large changes also require government policy and business action.
items.markingKey: Individual choices add up and influence markets, though large changes also require government policy and business action. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why a circular economy can reduce pressure on resources.
items.answer: Products are designed to last, be repaired and be recycled, so fewer new raw materials are extracted and less waste goes to landfill.

items.stem: Electricity generated from renewables in Germany was 36 TWh in 2000 and 267 TWh in 2023 (approx., German Federal Statistical Office). Calculate the percentage change.
items.markingKey: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100 (M1) = (267 − 36) ÷ 36 × 100 = +641.7% (A1). Dividing by the new value is a common error.

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why renewable resources can still be used unsustainably.
items.answer: If they are used faster than they regenerate – over-fishing, deforestation, over-pumping aquifers – stocks fall and may collapse, as with Newfoundland cod.

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "How sustainable is the use of groundwater for irrigation in the Punjab region of India?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Collect Central Ground Water Board data on water-table depth; read two reports; map affected districts; calculate the rate of fall; compare with recharge; evaluate data sources; cite in APA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Collect Central Ground Water Board data on water-table depth; read two reports; map affected districts; calculate the rate of fall; compare with recharge; evaluate data sources; cite in APA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.
